around.headline: Two women steal four gold bangles worth Rs 12 lakh from a Bengaluru showroom
around.summary: Two women reportedly stole four gold bangles worth about Rs 12 lakh from a jewellery showroom in Bengaluru, per today's report. around.summary: A man was caught after entering a PG room and stealing sanitary pads in Bengaluru, per today's report. If you live in a PG, lock your room even for short trips out and flag any stranger loitering in the corridors to your warden right away.

around.headline: Bengaluru roads get Rs 8,000 crore boost; potholes to be fixed by September-end
around.summary: The state has approved an Rs 8,000 crore package for Bengaluru's roads, with a target to clear potholes by the end of September, per today's report. Worth noting the deadline — it's the date to hold your local civic body to if a pothole on your route is still unfilled.

around.headline: Citizens form human chain at Lalbagh against 5% parkland amendment
around.summary: Bengaluru residents formed a human chain at Lalbagh today protesting a state amendment that would allow up to 5% of park land to be repurposed, per today's report. If you use Lalbagh or another city park regularly, this is the civic fight that could decide whether that green space stays protected.

around.headline: Nepal floods: 13 Karnataka residents stranded, 4 NRI pilgrims missing
around.summary: The chief minister's office confirmed 13 Karnataka residents are stranded and 4 NRI pilgrims are missing in Nepal's flash floods, with some Bengaluru families still awaiting word on parents caught in Tibet, per today's reports. If you have relatives travelling in the region, check in with them and watch for updates from the state helpline.

street_smart.title: You're home alone when a video call comes in from someone in a police uniform, sitting in front of an official-looking backdrop with a name plate. He says your Aadhaar and a courier addressed to you were used in a drug and money-laundering case, and you must stay on camera and tell no one — including family — while 'verification' happens. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: No single incident in today's feeds fits the choice-based trap format cleanly, so this rotates in from the evergreen list: digital-arrest scams. This specific mechanism — a fake police video call demanding the target stay on camera and isolated — hasn't been the street-smart scenario in the last three weeks of briefs (Aug 7–27), which instead covered rental/tenant traps, UPI QR fraud, auto/cab overcharging, two-wheeler theft and parking, phone snatching, loan-app harassment, credit-card skimming, medical emergencies, and several road-safety and civic-attack incidents.
street_smart.situation: The caller already has your name and phone number and claims to have your Aadhaar details on screen. He warns that hanging up or contacting anyone will be treated as evidence of guilt and could lead to your immediate arrest.

choices.text: Hang up immediately, and independently verify by calling the National Cyber Crime helpline (1930) or visiting cybercrime.gov.in — never a number the caller gave you.
choices.feedback: Correct. Indian law enforcement never conducts arrests, verification, or interrogation over a video call, and no genuine agency will ever tell you to stay silent and isolated. Verifying through an independently sourced number — not one the caller supplies — is what breaks the illusion of authority; the 1930 helpline and portal exist precisely for this.

choices.text: Stay on the call as instructed, keep your camera on, and avoid telling anyone since the caller warned that involving others would worsen your 'case'.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. The instruction to stay isolated and silent is the entire mechanism — it cuts you off from anyone who could tell you it's a scam while the caller pressures you toward a panicked money transfer or an OTP handover under the guise of 'clearing your name'.

choices.text: Ask the caller detailed questions about the case to see if his answers hold up before deciding what to do.
choices.feedback: Staying engaged at all keeps you on the hook — a rehearsed scammer can sound convincing on demand, and every extra minute on the call is a minute closer to being pressured into paying or sharing an OTP.

choices.text: Tell the caller you'll call back on the same number to think it over, then hang up.
choices.feedback: Calling back the same number just reconnects you to the scammer, not the police — genuine verification has to go through an independently sourced number, never the one the caller provided.

takeaways: No Indian police, ED, or CBI process happens over a video call, and none can legally order you to stay on camera under 'digital arrest' — the format itself is proof of a scam.
Report immediately to the National Cyber Crime helpline 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in, before any money moves — banks can sometimes freeze a fraudulent transfer within a short window if reported fast.
If a caller pressures you to isolate from family or friends, that instruction alone is the biggest red flag, regardless of how official they sound or look on screen.
